WalkthroughText: When you call a void method and pass it an object, Java copies the reference — the arrow that points to the object on the heap — into the method's parameter variable. Both the caller's variable and the parameter now point to the exact same object, so any change you make to that object's fields through the parameter (like calling a setter) is visible back in the caller. However, if inside the method you reassign the parameter itself to point to a different object, you're only redirecting that parameter's arrow; the caller's original variable still points at the original object, completely unaffected. This is the key distinction between mutating an object versus reassigning a reference variable.

PracticeItems.Explanation: myDog and the parameter d both start out pointing to the same Dog object because Java copies the reference (its address), not the object. Calling d.setName("Rex") follows that shared reference and changes the object's field, so myDog also sees the change. But the line d = new Dog("Buddy") only reassigns the local variable d to a brand-new object; it does not affect what myDog points to, since myDog's own stack cell was never touched. So the answer is Rex, not Buddy or Fido.

When resetCounter(myCounter) is called, the parameter c is a separate stack variable that is initialized with a copy of the reference stored in myCounter — both point to the same Counter object at first. Inside the method, c = new Counter() only changes where the local variable c points; it creates a new object on the heap and points c's arrow at it, but myCounter's arrow in the caller's frame is untouched and still points at the original object whose count is 2. Therefore 2 is printed, not 0.

PracticeItems.Prompt: Which statement correctly describes what happens on the call stack when a reference-type argument (like an object) is passed to a void method parameter in Java?
Choices: A brand-new copy of the entire object is created on the heap for the method to use
The parameter variable in the new stack frame stores a copy of the reference (arrow) to the same heap object as the argument
The method parameter becomes an alias that shares the same stack memory cell as the argument variable
No new stack frame is created since void methods do not return a value
PracticeItems.Explanation: Java always passes arguments by value. For reference types, the 'value' that gets copied into the new stack frame's parameter cell is the reference itself (the arrow to the heap object), not the object's data and not a shared memory cell. This is why mutating the object through the parameter affects the caller's object, but reassigning the parameter to a new object does not. Every method call, void or not, creates its own new stack frame.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: We start in main with a Dog object already created; myDog points to it on the heap.
We call changeName(myDog), so a new stack frame is pushed for the method.
The parameter d is initialized by copying myDog's reference — d now points to the SAME Dog object, dog1.
Notice: myDog in main and d in changeName are two separate stack cells, but their arrows point to the exact same heap object.
Inside the method, d.setName("Rex") follows d's arrow to dog1 and changes its name field directly.
Since myDog's arrow also points to dog1, this change is visible to main too — the object was mutated, not replaced.
Now the method executes d = new Dog("Buddy"), creating a brand-new Dog object on the heap.
This assignment only redirects d's own arrow to point at the new object dog2 — it does not touch myDog's stack cell at all.
The method finishes and its stack frame is popped off; d disappears entirely, along with its arrow to dog2.
Back in main, myDog's arrow was never redirected — it still points to dog1, which now has the name 'Rex' because that field was mutated earlier.
